answer_key.title: Empire Invoke SMBExec
answer_key.description: This dataset represents adversaries remotely creating and starting a service via RPC methods over SMB named pipes such as svcctl.

verdict.assessment: An attacker used compromised credentials (pgustavo) to execute an encoded PowerShell payload via SMBExec on WORKSTATION6, establishing persistence through a service and disabling script block logging, then initiating outbound C2 communication. The same attacker also attempted to build a reverse shell on WORKSTATION5 using raw socket operations.

findings.name: Pass the Hash
findings.behavior: pgustavo's credentials and NTLM hash were used via Invoke-SMBExec to execute an encoded PowerShell payload on WORKSTATION6 (172.18.39.6:445), establishing lateral movement from WORKSTATION5.
findings.reasoning: The evidence shows pgustavo's NTLM hash (81d310fa34e6a56a31145445891bb7b8) was used via Invoke-SMBExec to authenticate to WORKSTATION6, resulting in a network logon (LogonType 3) without a corresponding interactive logon. This is pass-the-hash lateral movement, not SMB share access or forced authentication.

findings.name: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
findings.behavior: A service named PGUJLOAKFQFVOMHGFQPX was installed on WORKSTATION6 by pgustavo with an encoded PowerShell payload, and script block logging was disabled via reflection to hide execution.
findings.reasoning: The operator disabled PowerShell script block logging via reflection to hide execution of the encoded payload. This is defense impairment—specifically disabling a logging mechanism—not the delivery or execution of the payload itself. T1562.008 (Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Logging) directly captures the adversary's objective of hiding their tracks by manipulating Windows logging infrastructure.

findings.name: DNS
findings.behavior: PowerShell on WORKSTATION6 initiated an outbound connection to 10.10.10.5:80 (likely C2), and on WORKSTATION5 a PowerShell script created a TCPClient socket for reverse shell communication.
findings.reasoning: The evidence shows PowerShell establishing outbound C2 communication to 10.10.10.5:80 and a reverse shell socket being created via TCPClient, indicating application layer protocol usage for command and control. This is application layer data exfiltration/C2 rather than multi-stage channels, proxy setup, or remote access tool deployment—the operator is using PowerShell itself as the C2 mechanism over HTTP/TCP.
